summary: This note, drawn from a Wikipedia article on the Sahara, describes the desert's northern boundary and the ecoregions around it. It explains that botanical and climatic criteria (date palm cultivation, esparto grass range, and the 100 mm isohyet) mark the northern limit. It then covers Ottoman control of the northern fringe in the 16th century and the South Saharan steppe ecoregion between the Sahara and the Sahel.
one_line: Describes the Sahara's northern limits, Ottoman-era control of its northern fringe, and the South Saharan steppe ecoregion.
key_facts: According to the botanical criteria of Frank White and geographer Robert Capot-Rey, the northern limit of the Sahara corresponds to the northern limit of date palm cultivation.
The southern limit of the range of esparto, a grass typical of the Mediterranean climate portion of the Maghreb and Iberia, also marks the northern limit of the Sahara.
The northern limit of the Sahara also corresponds to the 100 mm (3.9 in) isohyet of annual precipitation.
In the 16th century, coastal regencies in present-day Algeria and Tunisia, parts of present-day Libya, and the semi-autonomous kingdom of Egypt were occupied by the Ottoman Empire.
From 1517, Egypt was a valued part of the Ottoman Empire, giving the Ottomans control over the Nile Valley, the east Mediterranean and North Africa.
Trade under the Ottoman Empire exploited land routes to handle spices, gold and silk from the East, manufactures from Europe, and the slave and gold traffic from Africa.
Under Ottoman rule, Arabic continued as the local language and Islamic culture was much reinforced.
The Sahel and southern Sahara regions were home to several independent states or to roaming Tuareg clans.
The South Saharan steppe and woodlands ecoregion is a narrow band running east and west between the hyper-arid Sahara and the Sahel savannas to the south.
Movements of the equatorial Intertropical Convergence Zone (ITCZ) bring summer rains during July and August.
Summer rains in the South Saharan steppe average 100 to 200 mm (3.9 to 7.9 in) but vary greatly from year to year.
Summer rains sustain summer pastures of grasses and herbs, with dry woodlands and shrublands along seasonal watercourses.
The South Saharan steppe and woodlands ecoregion covers 1,101,700 km2 (425,400 mi2) in Algeria, Chad, Mali, Mauritania, and Sudan.
The northern Sahara borders Mediterranean forest, woodland, and scrub ecoregions, which have hot summers and cool, rainy winters.
